thread.title: A New Way to Rank the Risks of the FAANG Stocks

title: A New Way to Rank the Risks of the FAANG Stocks
text:
A New Way to Rank the Risks of the Big Tech Stocks By Oct. 19, 2018 5:51 p.m. ET Order Reprints Pawan Sharma Text size
Risk, in Wall Street parlance, is volatility. Higher volatility in a stock equals higher potential losses, and, as conventional wisdom dictates, investors must adjust their return expectations accordingly. That’s only half of the risk story. Volatility, beta, r-squared, or whatever market risk metrics you prefer, rely on backward-looking trading data and fail to capture what Donald Rumsfeld once called “unknown unknowns.”
Nowhere is this more obvious than with the highflying tech trade. A year ago, Facebook ’s global dominance made it the perfect stock. Today, that dominance has exposed the company to security issues and privacy concerns. Those new risks have caused Facebook (ticker: FB) to underperform the market and the other FAANG stocks year to date.
Then take Super Micro Computer (SMCI). Traditional risk metrics like beta or stock volatility indicated that Super Micro—a server and data-storage company—was actually less risky than in previous years. The stock had never moved more than 27% in a given day. But Super Micro’s servers became the centerpiece of a Bloomberg Businessweek investigation into Chinese espionage. The stock dropped 41% in one day on the news.
In assessing the latest bout of market volatility, Barron’s decided to come up with a more systematic approach to measuring FAANG risk . We went through a couple of exercises.
First, we tried to quantify the worst-case scenario. We reworked gross profit margins by thinking about how tech companies’ growing security issues could affect consumer behavior and company expenses. Our equation spit out $600 billion in market value at risk, given the profit hit if tech companies have to rethink security policies and supply chains. It’s not realistic to think we hit the nail on the head, but the exercise offers a way to account for news events—and events that could happen in the future—and their impact on stocks.
The second thing we did was create a FAANG risk score card, listing how Facebook, Amazon.com (AMZN), Apple (AAPL), Netflix (NFLX), and Alphabet ’s Google (GOOGL) fare on nine issues that have been discussed by analysts, the press, or politicians in the past year, including advertising reliance, regulations, antitrust issues, new tariffs, potential hardware hacking, privacy concerns, competition, valuation relative to tech averages and company history, and potential for data breaches.
For the most part, the market has adjusted appropriately to higher regulatory and privacy concerns. Witness Facebook’s and Google’s underperformance; both face the greatest risk in our scoring. Rating the FAANGs — A Barron’s Risk Score
Yet even our method is backward-looking, and we picked risks that have crept into the zeitgeist over the past year. The key is to evaluate how risks are likely to change in the future, if not to predict new risks. But our score card is still a good starting place, particularly when using it to think about how risks may change over the coming year.
Take tariffs. Industrial stocks have been affected now that companies are blaming higher raw material and component costs for weaker margins. Industrial multiples have clearly been affected. The industrial portion of the S&P 500 was trading at 17 times forward estimated earnings a year ago and now exchanges hands for 15 times earnings.
But what is the next stage in a U.S.-China trade war? If you believe Nafta 2.0 is a template for Chinese talks, then trade fears should subside after some limited announcements about market access and intellectual-property protection. That would fuel a relief rally in industrial stocks.
Tariffs are not only an industrial issue. Apple has said it views tariffs as a tax on the consumer, but management hasn’t updated its views since a July conference call. That took place before the latest levies went into effect. Analysts are likely to press Apple for more details when the company discusses results on Nov. 1. Is Risk Going to Rise or Fade for Each Firm
When it comes to privacy and government intervention, Apple and Netflix seem more insulated than peers. Both have been committed to protecting data. While that’s not entirely under their control, their business models are less driven by data and ads . Ad-driven Alphabet and Facebook are on the other side of that risk trade.
What about antitrust? Amazon’s retail dominance isn’t likely to change soon. Consider that analysts estimate that there are 60 million to 90 million Prime members in the U.S., and 120 million households. Amazon is still building out its grocery business, and a recent study said that 65% of Prime members would bank with Amazon. At some point, that dominance is likely to put Amazon in regulators’ crosshairs, if it’s not already there.
We asked each of the FAANGs for comment about new risks. Facebook and Amazon declined, and the others did not return messages.
Netflix emerged as the winner in our initial risk assessment. It’s less vulnerable to privacy and trade issues. But its risks are mounting. The stock is up 74% year to date and its price/earnings multiple has gone to 73 times from 50. And next year, Netflix is likely to meet its fiercest competition to date, when Disney launches its new streaming service.
